title: Altitude Training and Iron: Why Ferritin Matters
excerpt: Low ferritin may blunt the benefit of altitude training. What the research shows, and why to test your iron before supplementing, on medical advice.
body:
Iron matters for altitude training. Part of how your body adapts to thinner air is by making more red blood cells, and that process needs iron. If your iron stores are low, you may get less benefit from an altitude block.

The research is mixed. In one study of endurance athletes at 2,500 m, those with low ferritin (the body's iron store) did not increase their red cell volume over four weeks, unlike athletes with normal ferritin. Iron supplementation brought their ferritin back up. However, a study of 107 altitude camps by world-class endurance athletes found that pre-camp ferritin and iron supplements were not related to the increase in hemoglobin mass in athletes whose iron stores were already normal. So low ferritin may blunt the response, while normal stores appear to be enough.

If you're planning an altitude block:

  • Have your ferritin tested beforehand, through your doctor.
  • Take iron supplements only if a doctor advises it. Iron you don't need can cause side effects, and too much is harmful.
  • Include iron-rich foods in your diet, and avoid drastic changes to how you eat in the middle of a training camp.

Sources: Iron insufficiency diminishes the erythropoietic response to moderate altitude; Pre-altitude ferritin and iron supplement dose; Believe in the Run, episode 123
keyTakeaway: Get your ferritin tested before an altitude block, and take iron only if a doctor advises it.
